newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy Ross to seek to revive Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross to seek to revive Mideast talks.

text.p: The United States announced Monday it was sending special envoy Dennis Ross back to the Middle East this week for talks with Israeli and Palestinian leaders on reviving the stalled peace process.

U.S. officials said Ross would leave Tuesday evening and return by the weekend after talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. Ross is expected to fly to Tel Aviv.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, announcing the trip, said the talks would focus "on how to stem violence and what steps they are prepared to take to stop the deterioration and lay the basis for making the peace process work again."

U.S. President Bill Clinton would then decide "what the United States can and will do to re-establish the credibility of the process", Albright told reporters before a meeting with Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec.

Israeli-Palestinian talks have been at a standstill since January, in part due to the start of work on a new 6,500-unit Israeli housing project in mainly Arab East Jerusalem, which has led to almost daily Palestinian demonstrations.
Last week Netanyahu and a team of senior Palestinian negotiators paid successive visits to Washington to press their separate conditions for resuming peace talks and hear U.S. proposals.

Netanyahu demanded that the Palestinians stop violence and terrorism, while the Palestinians insisted that Israel halt its housing project begun on March 18 on a Jerusalem hill known to Jews as Har Homa and to Arabs as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
U.S. officials worry that relations between the two sides are deteriorating rapidly, putting in jeopardy the entire peace process launched by the 1993 and 1995 Oslo accords.

"The president and I have been very concerned about the recent developments in the Middle East," Albright said. "There has been a serious deterioration in the level of trust and confidence and in the ability of the parties to pursue peace."
Albright said the meeting between Ross and Arafat was likely to take place in Gaza, but gave no further details.

Ross, who brokered an Israeli-Palestinian deal in January for an Israeli troop withdrawal from most of the West Bank city of Hebron, made a subsequent visit to the region last month, with no visible signs of success.
Albright did not say whether she herself had any plans to visit the Middle East, something she has not done since she succeeded Warren Christopher as secretary of state in January.

As a way out of the deadlock, Netanyahu has proposed that Israel and the Palestinians should proceed immediately to negotiations on outstanding issues and try to wrap them up in six months instead of in 1999, as originally planned.

The Palestinians have reacted with suspicion to the idea although one negotiator, Saeb Erekat, hinted in Washington last week they might be prepared to consider speeding up talks provided Israel did not duck out of existing commitments.
Egypt said Monday it would launch a diplomatic campaign to lobby Washington and the European Union for initiatives to salvage the peace process.
Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said presidential adviser Osama el-Baz would visit Washington Tuesday to meet Ross.
